1	# Developer Workforce & Compensation Trends — 2024 Stack Overflow Survey
     2	
     3	## Source
     4	https://survey.stackoverflow.co/2024/work
     5	
     6	## Employment Status
     7	
     8	84% of the 65,437 respondents are currently working (full-time, part-time, or freelancing). Full-time employment is the dominant mode at 69%, followed by independent contracting/freelancing at 16.4% and full-time students at 13.2%.
     9	
    10	In the United States specifically, full-time employment dropped from 69% in 2023 to 64.8% in 2024. In the U.K. and Ukraine, non-full-time respondents lean toward independent contracting, while in Germany and India they are more likely to be full-time students.
    11	
    12	## Work Environment Trends
    13	
    14	Hybrid work remains the most common arrangement at 42%, consistent with 2023. Remote work accounts for 38%. In-person work has risen for the third consecutive year — from 15% in 2022 to 16% in 2023 to 20% in 2024 — signaling a gradual return-to-office trend.
    15	
    16	## Company Size
    17	
    18	47% of respondents work for organizations with fewer than 100 employees. The distribution across 42,827 respondents:
    19	
    20	| Company Size | Share |
    21	|---|---|
    22	| Freelancer / solo | 6.1% |
    23	| 2–9 employees | 10.4% |
    24	| 10–19 employees | 8.9% |
    25	| 20–99 employees | 21.2% |
    26	| 100–499 employees | 18.5% |
    27	| 500–999 employees | 6.7% |
    28	| 1,000–4,999 employees | 11.0% |
    29	| 5,000–9,999 employees | 3.8% |
    30	| 10,000+ employees | 11.4% |
    31	
    32	## Salary by Developer Type
    33	
    34	Median annual compensation (USD, all respondents) varies dramatically by role. The top and bottom roles are shown below (22,677 salary responses, 34.7% response rate):
    35	
    36	| Developer Type | Median Salary (USD) | Avg. Years Experience |
    37	|---|---|---|
    38	| Senior Executive | $127,388 | ~17 |
    39	| Dev Advocate | $124,203 | ~16 |
    40	| Manager | $115,999 | ~15 |
    41	| Dev Experience | $109,483 | ~12 |
    42	| SRE | $99,099 | ~10 |
    43	| Cloud Infra. Engineer | $96,666 | ~13 |
    44	| Blockchain | $85,925 | ~9 |
    45	| Product Manager | $80,000 | ~14 |
    46	| Full-stack | $63,333 | ~10 |
    47	| Front-end | $48,787 | ~8 |
    48	| Student | $15,466 | ~2 |
    49	
    50	Site reliability engineers and cloud infrastructure engineers are the highest-paid purely technical roles, reflecting their critical importance in keeping digital services running. Regionally, mobile developers earn more in the U.S., data engineers top the charts in Germany and Ukraine, and back-end developers lead in India and the U.K.
    51	
    52	![Salary by developer type — bar chart](./assets/figure_1.jpg)
    53	
    54	![Salary vs. experience by developer type — scatter plot](./assets/figure_2.jpg)
    55	
    56	## Salary by Programming Language
    57	
    58	Developers using niche functional languages earn the most. The overall reported salary range has dropped roughly $10K compared to 2023, now averaging $60–75K USD vs. $70–85K USD last year.
    59	
    60	| Language | Median Salary (USD) | Avg. Years Experience |
    61	|---|---|---|
    62	| Erlang | ~$97,000 | ~12 |
    63	| Clojure | ~$95,000 | ~11 |
    64	| Elixir | ~$93,000 | ~11 |
    65	| Perl | ~$90,000 | ~19 |
    66	| Ruby | ~$89,000 | ~11 |
    67	| Scala | ~$88,000 | ~9 |
    68	| Go | ~$76,000 | ~9 |
    69	| Python | ~$67,000 | ~9 |
    70	| JavaScript | ~$64,000 | ~10 |
    71	| PHP | ~$49,000 | ~10 |
    72	| Dart | ~$44,000 | ~8 |
    73	| Prolog | ~$43,000 | ~9 |
    74	
    75	![Salary vs. experience by language — scatter plot](./assets/figure_3.jpg)
    76	
    77	## Technology Purchasing Influence
    78	
    79	62% of respondents have influence over technology purchases at their organizations. Senior executives (99%), engineering managers (87%), and product managers (77%) wield the most influence. 60% of respondents prefer a build-and-buy approach over purely building or buying. Starting a free trial (75%) and asking other developers (73%) are the top methods for evaluating new tools.
    80	
    81	## Key Findings
    82	
    83	- **Full-time employment is softening**: U.S. full-time employment fell 4 percentage points year-over-year; freelancing and contracting remain significant at 16%+.
    84	- **In-person work is creeping back**: now at 20%, up from 15% in 2022, though hybrid (42%) still dominates.
    85	- **DevRel and leadership roles command premium pay**: Senior Executives ($127K), Dev Advocates ($124K), and Managers ($116K) top the salary chart, all with 15+ years average experience.
    86	- **Niche functional languages correlate with higher pay**: Erlang, Clojure, and Elixir developers earn >$93K median, while mainstream languages like JavaScript and PHP sit well below $65K.
    87	- **Developers are key purchase influencers**: with 62% having a say in tech buying decisions, vendor strategies should target individual contributors, not just management.

     6	description: "Create, inspect, and edit Microsoft PowerPoint presentations and PPTX decks with reliable layouts, templates, placeholders, notes, charts, and visual QA. Use when (1) the task is about PowerPoint or `.pptx`; (2) layouts, placeholders, notes, charts, comments, or template fidelity matter; (3) the deck must render cleanly after edits."
     7	changelog: Rebalanced the skill toward template inventory, layout mapping, and higher-signal QA after a stricter external audit.

     9	---
    10	
    11	## When to Use
    12	
    13	Use when the main artifact is a Microsoft PowerPoint presentation or `.pptx` deck, especially when layouts, templates, placeholders, notes, comments, charts, extraction, editing, or final visual quality matter.
    14	
    15	## Core Rules
    16	
    17	### 1. Choose the workflow before touching the deck
    18	
    19	- Reading text, editing an existing deck, rebuilding from a template, and creating from scratch are different jobs with different failure modes.
    20	- For text extraction or inspection, read the deck before editing it.
    21	- Text extraction plus thumbnail-style visual inspection is safer than editing from shape assumptions alone.
    22	- For template-driven work, inventory the deck before replacing content.
    23	- For deep edits, remember a `.pptx` file is OOXML with separate parts for slides, layouts, masters, media, notes, and comments.
    24	- If a template exists, template fidelity beats generic slide-design instincts.
    25	- Reusing or duplicating a good existing slide is often safer than rebuilding it and hoping the theme still matches.
    26	
    27	### 2. Inventory the deck before replacing content
    28	
    29	- Count the reusable layouts, real placeholders, notes, comments, media, and recurring typography or color patterns first.
    30	- Placeholder indexes and layout indexes are not portable assumptions.
    31	- Inspect the actual slide or template before targeting title, body, chart, or image shapes.
    32	- Speaker notes, comments, and linked assets can live outside the visible slide surface.
    33	- A missing or wrong placeholder target can silently land content in the wrong box or wrong layer.
    34	- Master and layout settings can override local slide edits, so the visible problem is not always on the slide you are editing.
    35	
    36	### 3. Match content to the actual placeholders
    37	
    38	- Count the actual content pieces before choosing a layout.
    39	- Pick layouts based on the real number of ideas, columns, images, or charts the slide needs.
    40	- Do not force two ideas into a three-column slide or cram dense text under a chart.
    41	- Category counts and data series lengths must match or charts will break in ugly ways.
    42	- Explicit sizing beats wishful thinking: text boxes, images, and charts need real space, not "it should fit".
    43	- Do not choose a layout with more placeholders than the content can meaningfully fill.
    44	- Quote layouts are for real quotes, and image-led layouts are for slides that actually have images.
    45	- For chart-, table-, or image-heavy slides, full-slide or two-column layouts are usually safer than stacking dense text above the visual.
    46	
    47	### 4. Preserve the deck's visual language
    48	
    49	- Theme, master, and layout files usually decide fonts, colors, and hierarchy more than any one slide does.
    50	- Start from the deck's actual theme, fonts, spacing, and aspect ratio instead of improvising a new style.
    51	- Reuse the deck's own alignment and spacing system instead of inventing a second visual language.
    52	- Use common fonts for portability and strong contrast for readability.
    53	- Preserve the template's visual logic first; originality matters less than not breaking the deck's existing language.
    54	- Combining slides from multiple sources requires normalizing themes, masters, and alignment afterward.
    55	
    56	### 5. Run content QA and visual QA separately
    57	
    58	- Text overflow, bad alignment, clipped shapes, weak contrast, and placeholder leftovers are normal first-pass failures.
    59	- Run both content QA and visual QA; missing text and broken layout are different failure classes.
    60	- Render or inspect the actual deck output before delivery when layout matters.
    61	- Search for leftover template junk, sample labels, and placeholder text before calling the deck finished.
    62	- Check notes, comments, labels, legends, and chart/table semantics separately from the visual pass.
    63	- A deck can pass text extraction and still fail on overlap, clipping, wrong theme inheritance, or broken notes.
    64	- Thumbnail grids and rendered slides usually reveal layout bugs faster than code or text inspection.
    65	- Assume the first render is wrong and do at least one fix-and-verify cycle before calling the deck finished.
    66	- Re-check affected slides after each fix because one spacing change often creates another issue.
    67	
    68	### 6. Keep decks portable and review-safe
    69	
    70	- Template masters can override direct edits in surprising ways.
    71	- Complex effects may degrade across PowerPoint, LibreOffice, and conversion pipelines, so keep important content robust without them.
    72	- Image sizing, font substitution, and placeholder mismatch are common reasons a deck looks good in code and bad on screen.
    73	- Notes, comments, linked media, and merged decks can stay broken even when the visible slide looks fine.
    74	
    75	## Common Traps
    76	
    77	- Placeholder text and sample charts often survive template reuse if not explicitly replaced.
    78	- Directly editing one slide can fail if the real issue lives in the master or layout.
    79	- Charts, icons, and text boxes need enough space; near-collisions are usually visible only after rendering.
    80	- Layout indexes vary by template, so built-in assumptions from one deck often break in another.
    81	- A missing placeholder or wrong shape target can silently put content in the wrong place.
    82	- Counting the text ideas after choosing the layout usually leads to empty placeholders, weak hierarchy, or leftover template junk.
    83	- Font substitution can move line breaks and wreck careful spacing.
    84	- Speaker notes, comments, and linked media can stay broken even when the visible slide looks fine.
    85	- A deck can pass text inspection and still fail visually because of overlap, contrast, or edge clipping.
    86	- Editing from one slide alone can miss the real source of truth in the theme, master, or layout definitions.
    87	- Choosing a quote, comparison, or multi-column layout without matching content usually makes the deck look templated rather than intentional.
    88	- Combining or duplicating slides without checking masters and themes can create subtle inconsistency slide by slide.
    89	- Aspect-ratio mismatches like `16:9` versus `4:3` can shift every placement decision even when each slide looks locally reasonable.
    90	
    91	## Related Skills
    92	Install with `clawhub install <slug>` if user confirms:
    93	- `documents` — Document workflows that often feed presentation content.
    94	- `design` — Visual direction and layout decisions.
    95	- `brief` — Concise business messaging for slide narratives.
    96

    98	
    99	- If useful: `clawhub star powerpoint-pptx`
   100	- Stay updated: `clawhub sync`

from pptx import Presentation
from pptx.util import Inches, Pt
from pptx.dml.color import RgbColor
from pptx.enum.text import PP_ALIGN, MSO_ANCHOR
from pptx.enum.shapes import MSO_SHAPE
from pptx.oxml.ns import nsmap
from pptx.oxml import parse_xml
from lxml import etree
import os

# Create presentation 16:9
prs = Presentation()
prs.slide_width = Inches(13.333)
prs.slide_height = Inches(7.5)

# Color palette (data-forward, professional)
DARK_BLUE = RgbColor(0x1A, 0x23, 0x7E)
TEAL = RgbColor(0x00, 0x8C, 0x8C)
LIGHT_TEAL = RgbColor(0x4F, 0xB8, 0xB8)
DARK_GRAY = RgbColor(0x33, 0x33, 0x33)
MEDIUM_GRAY = RgbColor(0x66, 0x66, 0x66)
LIGHT_GRAY = RgbColor(0xF5, 0xF5, 0xF5)
WHITE = RgbColor(0xFF, 0xFF, 0xFF)
ACCENT_ORANGE = RgbColor(0xE6, 0x5C, 0x00)

def add_title_shape(slide, left, top, width, height, text, font_size=Pt(32), bold=True, color=DARK_BLUE, align=PP_ALIGN.LEFT):
    shape = slide.shapes.add_textbox(left, top, width, height)
    tf = shape.text_frame
    tf.word_wrap = True
    p = tf.paragraphs[0]
    p.text = text
    p.font.size = font_size
    p.font.bold = bold
    p.font.color.rgb = color
    p.font.name = "Calibri"
    p.alignment = align
    return shape

def add_body_text(slide, left, top, width, height, text, font_size=Pt(16), color=DARK_GRAY, align=PP_ALIGN.LEFT, bullet=False):
    shape = slide.shapes.add_textbox(left, top, width, height)
    tf = shape.text_frame
    tf.word_wrap = True
    p = tf.paragraphs[0]
    p.text = text
    p.font.size = font_size
    p.font.color.rgb = color
    p.font.name = "Calibri"
    p.alignment = align
    if bullet:
        p.level = 0
    return shape

def add_bullet_list(slide, left, top, width, height, items, font_size=Pt(16), color=DARK_GRAY):
    shape = slide.shapes.add_textbox(left, top, width, height)
    tf = shape.text_frame
    tf.word_wrap = True
    for i, item in enumerate(items):
        if i == 0:
            p = tf.paragraphs[0]
        else:
            p = tf.add_paragraph()
        p.text = item
        p.font.size = font_size
        p.font.color.rgb = color
        p.font.name = "Calibri"
        p.level = 0
        p.space_after = Pt(10)
    return shape

# Helper to set solid fill on shape

def set_shape_fill(shape, color):
    shape.fill.solid()
    shape.fill.fore_color.rgb = color

# ============================
# Slide 1: Title Slide
# ============================
slide_layout = prs.slide_layouts[6]  # blank
slide1 = prs.slides.add_slide(slide_layout)

# Background bar
bar = slide1.shapes.add_shape(MSO_SHAPE.RECTANGLE, Inches(0), Inches(0), Inches(13.333), Inches(2.2))
set_shape_fill(bar, DARK_BLUE)
bar.line.fill.background()

# Title
title_shape = slide1.shapes.add_textbox(Inches(0.8), Inches(0.5), Inches(11.7), Inches(1.5))
tf = title_shape.text_frame
tf.word_wrap = True
p = tf.paragraphs[0]
p.text = "Developer Workforce & Compensation Trends"
p.font.size = Pt(40)
p.font.bold = True
p.font.color.rgb = WHITE
p.font.name = "Calibri"

# Subtitle
sub = slide1.shapes.add_textbox(Inches(0.8), Inches(1.6), Inches(11.7), Inches(0.6))
tf2 = sub.text_frame
tf2.word_wrap = True
p2 = tf2.paragraphs[0]
p2.text = "2024 Stack Overflow Survey"
p2.font.size = Pt(24)
p2.font.color.rgb = LIGHT_TEAL
p2.font.name = "Calibri"

# Metadata box
meta = slide1.shapes.add_shape(MSO_SHAPE.ROUNDED_RECTANGLE, Inches(0.8), Inches(3.0), Inches(5.5), Inches(2.0))
set_shape_fill(meta, LIGHT_GRAY)
meta.line.color.rgb = TEAL
meta_tf = meta.text_frame
meta_tf.word_wrap = True
mp = meta_tf.paragraphs[0]
mp.text = "65,437 respondents across 180+ countries"
mp.font.size = Pt(20)
mp.font.bold = True
mp.font.color.rgb = DARK_BLUE
mp.font.name = "Calibri"
mp.alignment = PP_ALIGN.CENTER

# Source
src = slide1.shapes.add_textbox(Inches(0.8), Inches(5.3), Inches(5.5), Inches(0.5))
src_tf = src.text_frame
sp = src_tf.paragraphs[0]
sp.text = "Source: survey.stackoverflow.co/2024/work"
sp.font.size = Pt(12)
sp.font.color.rgb = MEDIUM_GRAY
sp.font.name = "Calibri"
sp.alignment = PP_ALIGN.CENTER

# Right side image placeholder (using figure_1 as decorative)
# We'll add a small visual accent
accent = slide1.shapes.add_shape(MSO_SHAPE.RECTANGLE, Inches(7.0), Inches(3.0), Inches(5.5), Inches(3.5))
set_shape_fill(accent, WHITE)
accent.line.color.rgb = TEAL
accent.line.width = Pt(2)
acc_text = accent.text_frame
acc_text.word_wrap = True
ap = acc_text.paragraphs[0]
ap.text = "Data-Driven Insights for Engineering Leaders & HR Strategists"
ap.font.size = Pt(18)
ap.font.color.rgb = DARK_GRAY
ap.font.name = "Calibri"
ap.alignment = PP_ALIGN.CENTER

# ============================
# Slide 2: Employment Status Overview
# ============================
slide2 = prs.slides.add_slide(slide_layout)

# Header bar
hb2 = slide2.shapes.add_shape(MSO_SHAPE.RECTANGLE, Inches(0), Inches(0), Inches(13.333), Inches(1.1))
set_shape_fill(hb2, DARK_BLUE)
hb2.line.fill.background()
add_title_shape(slide2, Inches(0.5), Inches(0.25), Inches(12.3), Inches(0.7),
                "84% of Developers Are Working, but Full-Time Employment Dips in the U.S.",
                font_size=Pt(26), color=WHITE)

# Left: Global breakdown
left_title = add_body_text(slide2, Inches(0.5), Inches(1.4), Inches(5.8), Inches(0.4),
                           "Global Employment Status (65,437 respondents)", font_size=Pt(16), color=DARK_BLUE)
left_title.text_frame.paragraphs[0].font.bold = True

items2 = [
    "Full-time: 69% (dominant mode)",
    "Independent contracting / freelancing: 16.4%",
    "Full-time students: 13.2%",
    "Other / not working: 16%"
]
add_bullet_list(slide2, Inches(0.5), Inches(1.9), Inches(5.8), Inches(2.5), items2, font_size=Pt(15))

# Right: US drop
right_title = add_body_text(slide2, Inches(7.0), Inches(1.4), Inches(5.8), Inches(0.4),
                            "U.S. Full-Time Employment Shift", font_size=Pt(16), color=DARK_BLUE)
right_title.text_frame.paragraphs[0].font.bold = True

us_box = slide2.shapes.add_shape(MSO_SHAPE.ROUNDED_RECTANGLE, Inches(7.0), Inches(1.9), Inches(5.5), Inches(2.2))
set_shape_fill(us_box, LIGHT_GRAY)
us_box.line.color.rgb = ACCENT_ORANGE
us_tf = us_box.text_frame
us_tf.word_wrap = True
usp = us_tf.paragraphs[0]
usp.text = "↓ 4.2 percentage points"
usp.font.size = Pt(28)
usp.font.bold = True
usp.font.color.rgb = ACCENT_ORANGE
usp.font.name = "Calibri"
usp.alignment = PP_ALIGN.CENTER

usp2 = us_tf.add_paragraph()
usp2.text = "U.S. full-time employment dropped from 69% in 2023 to 64.8% in 2024"
usp2.font.size = Pt(15)
usp2.font.color.rgb = DARK_GRAY
usp2.font.name = "Calibri"
usp2.alignment = PP_ALIGN.CENTER

# Bottom note
add_body_text(slide2, Inches(0.5), Inches(4.5), Inches(12.3), Inches(0.8),
              "Note: In the U.K. and Ukraine, non-full-time respondents lean toward independent contracting; in Germany and India, they are more likely to be full-time students.",
              font_size=Pt(13), color=MEDIUM_GRAY)

# ============================
# Slide 3: Work Environment Shift
# ============================
slide3 = prs.slides.add_slide(slide_layout)

hb3 = slide3.shapes.add_shape(MSO_SHAPE.RECTANGLE, Inches(0), Inches(0), Inches(13.333), Inches(1.1))
set_shape_fill(hb3, DARK_BLUE)
